About.title: About StockLens
About.what: StockLens is a free learning tool made for the PMF Investment Society. It helps you read the key numbers of a listed company and form your own opinion.
About.advice: Everything here is educational. StockLens is not a broker, you cannot buy or sell anything, and nothing on this site tells you what to do with your money. Analyst opinions are arguments to evaluate, not instructions.
About.data: Prices and company figures come from Yahoo Finance through an unofficial channel. They can be delayed (the delay is shown next to each price), incomplete or wrong. When a figure is missing we say so instead of guessing.
About.storageTitle: What is stored in your browser
About.storage: No account, no ads, no tracking, no analytics. Your watchlist, recently viewed companies, recent searches, notes, buy/hold/sell picks, value estimates and the last class link are saved in this browser only (localStorage), so we never see them and they do not follow you to another device. A one-time flag remembers that you saw the opening animation during this visit (sessionStorage). You can erase everything at any time by clearing this site's data in your browser settings.
About.cookies: StockLens sets no cookie of its own for tracking. If the club organiser switches on a shared club code, one strictly necessary cookie remembers that you entered it for 30 days.
About.server: The site is hosted on Vercel. Like any web host, Vercel receives your IP address and the pages you request, and keeps technical logs under its own policy. StockLens uses your IP address only for a short-lived counter that limits abuse. We do not build profiles, and we do not store your notes or picks on any server.
About.aiTitle: How the AI text is made
About.ai: The company explanation and the bull / bear / hold arguments are written by AI models (Google Gemini, with Groq and Gemma as back-ups). They receive only public market data and public company descriptions for the company you are viewing. They never receive your notes, picks, IP address or anything about you. The AI can still be wrong, so every number it quotes is inserted by our code from the data on the page, and its text is a starting point to question, not a source of truth. Google's free tier may use submitted content to improve its products, which is one more reason nothing personal is ever sent.
About.audience: StockLens is a classroom tool for adults (18+) of the PMF Investment Society, who the professor has confirmed live outside the EEA, Switzerland and the UK. It is not indexed by search engines and is not meant for the general public or for minors.
About.terms: Use StockLens for learning only, for free and for non-commercial purposes. It is provided as is, with no guarantee that it is accurate, complete, on time or always available, and you use it at your own risk. Do not copy, resell or republish its data, and do not automate requests to it. Nothing is bought or sold here and no real money is involved. For questions or to ask for your data to be removed, contact your professor or the club organiser.
About.credits: Charts are drawn with TradingView Lightweight Charts, used under its licence.

eps.title: Earnings per share (EPS)
eps.meaning: Profit for each share, last quarter, compared with what analysts expected.
eps.definition: The profit the company made, divided among all its shares. Also called BPA in French.
eps.rule: Beating or missing by a few percent is common. Look at several quarters, not just one.

pe.title: P/E ratio
pe.meaning: Years of profit it would take to earn back the price of one share.
pe.definition: How many times the yearly profit per share the market pays for one share. Read it as the number of years of profit needed to earn your money back.
pe.rule: A high P/E often means investors expect strong growth, a low one can mean low expectations or doubts. Compare with similar companies.

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.meaning: The money the company earned by selling its products or services.
revenue.definition: Everything customers paid the company during the period, before any cost is removed. Also called sales.
revenue.formula: Price of each sale × number of sales
revenue.rule: Growing revenue is only good news if profit follows. Compare with the same period last year.

operating.title: Operating profit
operating.meaning: What is left after the costs of running the business, before interest and tax.
operating.definition: The profit from the company's everyday activity.
operating.formula: Revenue − operating costs. The margin is operating profit ÷ revenue.
operating.rule: Margins differ a lot between industries. Compare a company with its competitors.

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.meaning: The cash left after paying to run and maintain the business.
fcf.definition: Cash that came in, minus cash that went out to run the company and to pay for equipment. It is what the company is really free to use.
fcf.formula: Cash from operations − investment in equipment and buildings
fcf.rule: A company can show a profit but little free cash flow, for example when it invests heavily. Look at both.

marketCap.title: Market capitalisation
marketCap.meaning: What the stock market says the whole company is worth today.
marketCap.definition: The price of one share multiplied by the number of shares. It is the price of the whole company, not the profit.
marketCap.rule: Companies above roughly 10 billion are often called large caps. Smaller companies tend to move more.

Quiz.title: Test yourself
Quiz.intro: Short questions built from this company's numbers. No score and no timer: the explanation is the point.
Quiz.ruleNote: This answer follows a rule of thumb, not a law: real companies can be exceptions.
Quiz.none: There is not enough data on this company for a quiz right now.
Quiz.notAdvice: Practice questions about reading numbers. They say nothing about what to do with a share.

pe_years.question: {name}'s P/E is {pe}. Roughly how many years of its current profit would it take to earn back the price of one share?

options.years: About {n, plural, one {# year} other {# years}}

explain.default: The P/E is the share price divided by the profit per share, so a P/E of {pe} means about {n} years of today's profit to match today's price. It is a way of reading the price, not a promise: profits change from year to year.

pe_reading.question: {name}'s P/E is {pe}. As a rule of thumb, what is the market usually pricing in?

options.growth: Strong growth to come: investors accept paying a lot for each unit of profit today
options.steady: Stability, or some doubts: investors do not pay much for each unit of profit today

explain.growth: A P/E of {pe} is high. It often means the market expects profits to grow a lot. That is a rule of thumb, not a law: a high P/E can also simply mean the share is expensive, so compare with companies in the same sector.
explain.steady: A P/E of {pe} is low. It often goes with a steady business that grows slowly, or with doubts about the future. That is a rule of thumb, not a law: compare with similar companies before drawing a conclusion.

eps_surprise.question: For the quarter ending {quarter}, {name} reported earnings per share (EPS) of {actual}. Analysts expected {estimate}. Compared with the expectation, is this a beat, a miss or in line?

options.inline: In line: almost the same as expected

explain.beat: {actual} is higher than the {estimate} analysts expected, so this is a beat of {pct} against the expected figure. A beat compares a result with expectations: it does not forecast what the share price will do.
explain.miss: {actual} is lower than the {estimate} analysts expected, so this is a miss of {pct} against the expected figure. A miss compares a result with expectations: it does not forecast what the share price will do.
explain.inline: {actual} is almost identical to the {estimate} analysts expected, so we call it in line. Where exactly to draw that line (here, about half a percent) is a convention, not a law.

forward_vs_trailing.question: {name} has a trailing P/E of {trailing} (based on the last 12 months of profit) and a forward P/E of {forward} (based on the profit analysts expect over the next 12 months). The share price is the same in both. What does the difference suggest?

options.higher: Analysts expect a higher profit over the next 12 months than over the last 12
options.lower: Analysts expect a lower profit over the next 12 months than over the last 12

explain.higher: Same price, smaller P/E: the profit it is divided by must be bigger. A forward P/E ({forward}) below the trailing P/E ({trailing}) means analysts expect the profit per share to rise. These are forecasts, and forecasts are often wrong.
explain.lower: Same price, bigger P/E: the profit it is divided by must be smaller. A forward P/E ({forward}) above the trailing P/E ({trailing}) means analysts expect the profit per share to fall. These are forecasts, and forecasts are often wrong.

dividend_income.question: {name}'s dividend yield is {yield}. If the dividend stays the same, about how much would shares worth {stake} pay in dividends over a year?

explain.default: The dividend yield is the yearly dividend divided by the share price: {yield} of {stake} is about {amount} a year. The company decides the dividend and can change or stop it, so the yield is a snapshot, not a promise.

payout_ratio.question: {name} paid out about {ratio} of its profit as dividends (the payout ratio, DPR). As a rule of thumb, what does that suggest?

options.low: It keeps most of its profit to reinvest or set aside
options.mid: It shares roughly half of its profit and keeps the rest
options.high: It pays out most of its profit, which leaves little cushion if profit falls

explain.low: At {ratio}, most of the profit stays in the company. Rule of thumb, not a law: under about 35% is often read as "keeps most", between 35% and 70% as "shares about half", over 70% as "pays out most". Sectors differ a lot.
explain.mid: At {ratio}, the profit is roughly shared between shareholders and the company. Rule of thumb, not a law: under about 35% is often read as "keeps most", between 35% and 70% as "shares about half", over 70% as "pays out most". Sectors differ a lot.
explain.high: At {ratio}, most of the profit goes to shareholders. Rule of thumb, not a law: under about 35% is often read as "keeps most", between 35% and 70% as "shares about half", over 70% as "pays out most". Sectors differ a lot.

price_vs_target.question: {name} trades at {price}. The average price target of professional analysts is {mean} (their targets range from {low} to {high}). How does the average target compare with the price?

explain.above: The average target, {mean}, is {gap} above the price, {price}. Targets are analysts' opinions, often revised and often wrong: this compares two numbers and says nothing certain about where the price will go.
explain.below: The average target, {mean}, is {gap} below the price, {price}. Targets are analysts' opinions, often revised and often wrong: this compares two numbers and says nothing certain about where the price will go.
explain.same: The average target, {mean}, is within {band} of the price, {price}, so we call it about the same. That {band} margin is a rule of thumb, not a law. Targets are analysts' opinions, often revised and often wrong.

market_cap_size.question: {name} has a market capitalisation of {cap}. Which group do investors usually put it in?

options.small: A small or mid-size company (under 10 billion)

explain.small: Market capitalisation is the share price times the number of shares: the price of the whole company, here {cap}. These groups are conventions, not laws: banks and indices draw the lines in slightly different places. The lines used here are a rule of thumb for USD, EUR, GBP and CHF.
explain.large: Market capitalisation is the share price times the number of shares: the price of the whole company, here {cap}. These groups are conventions, not laws: banks and indices draw the lines in slightly different places. The lines used here are a rule of thumb for USD, EUR, GBP and CHF.
explain.mega: Market capitalisation is the share price times the number of shares: the price of the whole company, here {cap}. These groups are conventions, not laws: banks and indices draw the lines in slightly different places. The lines used here are a rule of thumb for USD, EUR, GBP and CHF.

operating_margin.question: {name}'s operating margin is {margin}. Out of every 100 of sales, about how much is left as operating profit, before interest and tax?

explain.default: Operating margin is operating profit divided by sales. {margin} means about {n} of operating profit for every 100 of sales; the rest pays the costs of running the business. Normal margins differ a lot between sectors, so compare a company with its competitors.

operating_loss.question: {name}'s operating margin is {margin}, a negative number. What does that mean?

options.costs: The costs of running the business are higher than its sales
options.cash: The company has more cash than debt
options.sales: Sales fell compared with last year

explain.default: Operating margin is operating profit divided by sales. A negative margin means the operating costs are higher than the sales, so the business makes an operating loss. Many young companies run at a loss while they grow: a loss is a fact to understand, not a verdict.

free_cash_flow.question: {name}'s latest free cash flow is {fcf}. What does the sign tell you?

options.in: More cash came in than went out, after paying to run and maintain the business
options.out: More cash went out than came in, after paying to run and maintain the business

explain.positive: Free cash flow is the cash coming in minus the cash going out to run the business and pay for equipment. A positive figure ({fcf}) means cash was left over. It covers one period only, so look at several.
explain.negative: Free cash flow is the cash coming in minus the cash going out to run the business and pay for equipment. A negative figure ({fcf}) means more cash left than arrived. That happens when a company invests heavily to grow, or when it struggles: you need the story behind the number.

Safety.title: Margin of safety
Safety.intro: What do you think one share is really worth? Type your own estimate and see how far the price is from it.
Safety.label: Your estimate of what one share is worth, in {currency}
Safety.hint: Use your own reasoning: for example, the profit per share you find realistic times a P/E you find reasonable.
Safety.subunit: Prices on this page are in {currency}, not in {quotedAs} ({factor} {quotedAs} = 1 {currency}). Type your estimate in {currency}.
Safety.saved: Your estimate is only stored in this browser.

errors.invalid: That does not look like a number. Try something like 120 or 12,50.
errors.not_positive: The estimate must be greater than zero.
errors.too_large: That number is too large for the price of one share.

Safety.far: Your estimate is very far from the current price. Check the number and the currency.
Safety.below: The price is {pct} below your estimate: on your numbers, there is a margin of safety.
Safety.above: The price is {pct} above your estimate: on your numbers, there is no margin of safety.
Safety.about_equal: The price is about the same as your estimate (less than half a percent apart).
Safety.gapAbove: Your estimate is {pct} above the current price.
Safety.gapBelow: Your estimate is {pct} below the current price.
Safety.notAdvice: This is your estimate, not a prediction or advice. If your estimate is wrong, the margin is wrong too.
Safety.learn: What is a margin of safety?
